open-question.recommendation: A task's commit is usually unpushed while its mission runs, so only a local target always works, and one read-only git show document holds the subject, the verified bar, and the patch with the brief among its removed lines together, for the least code of the in-editor forms.

open-question.question: The runner of Gurita for VS Code waits for a keypress after every chain and after every looped task run. A new setting is to close the terminal by itself when a chain ran all its lines. Does the setting also close the terminal of a looped task run that completed every task?
open-question.alternative: The one new setting governs both kinds of run. With it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` (the runner's `finished` outcome, reached once no `##` heading is left in `TASKS_TODO.md`) prints its report and exits without waiting for a keypress, so its terminal closes and the page unblocks. A loop that stopped (an unresolved assignment, a task that did not end on `Task completed.`, or an unreadable task list) still waits for a keypress, as a stopped chain does. One rule for every run: `run_chain` and `run_loop` already end the same way (report, `wait_for_key`, exit 0 when finished), so the setting skips the same wait at both, and the looped run, which is the long unattended run where an unblocked page on success matters most, gets the benefit too. The loop's closing report (`Tasks completed: N`) and every task session's output vanish with the terminal on success, leaving only the commits and the refreshed page as the record; the setting's description and the README must say it reaches looped runs, since the tracker entry names only chains.

The setting closes only a chain's terminal. A looped task run keeps waiting for a keypress after its report whatever the setting says and however the loop ended, exactly as today. Follows the tracker entry's wording literally and keeps the one run that can complete many tasks unattended always reviewable at its end, with the runner's loop path left unchanged. A loop that completed every task still leaves the mission's page blocked until someone presses a key, the very wait the setting exists to remove, and a user who turned the setting on is likely to read the loop's lingering terminal as the setting not working.

Looped runs get a setting of their own beside the chain one: with it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` exits without waiting for a keypress, while a stopped loop still waits; the chain setting does not reach loops and the loop setting does not reach chains. Lets a user auto-close short chains while still reviewing the output of a long multi-task run, or the reverse, without either choice being forced on the other. Adds a second setting to the manifest, its description, and the README for a distinction few users are likely to want, and needs a default of its own, which depends on how the default of the chain setting is settled.

open-question.question: Gurita for VS Code is to re-read the missions when git state changes through a commit, a pull, or a branch switch made outside its own runs; today its one file watcher covers the mission documents only. How does the extension learn of such a change: by watching files inside the repository's `.git` directory, or through the API of VS Code's built-in Git extension?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It reuses the session's own watcher, debounce, and full re-read with a pure event mapping the tests can cover, and it works whatever the built-in Git extension's enablement says, in keeping with an extension that already runs git itself; a ref layout the filter does not know leaves today's behaviour, a stale page until Refresh.
open-question.alternative: A second `vscode.workspace.createFileSystemWatcher` is created beside the mission-document watcher in `src/pane.ts`, over the repository's git directory as `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` (and `--git-common-dir` for a linked worktree's refs) resolves it from the project root, covering only the files that move `HEAD`: `HEAD`, `refs/heads/**`, and `packed-refs`, with lock files, the index, objects, and remote refs ignored. Each event is mapped, by a pure function beside `eventEffect` in `src/refresh.ts`, to an effect asking for a full re-read (`live: true`), so it goes through the existing 300 ms debounce and re-runs what Refresh runs. No other extension is used. It adds no dependency: it works whatever the built-in Git extension's settings, enablement, or repository detection say, reuses the one mechanism the session already has (watcher, debounce, full re-read), and its event-to-effect mapping is a pure function testable under `node:test` like `refresh.test.ts`. The extension takes on git's on-disk layout as its own contract: a worktree's `.git` is a file pointing elsewhere, refs may be packed or, under git's newer reftable backend, written to no `refs/heads` file at all, and a git directory outside the workspace folder needs a watcher outside it, so a layout the filter does not know leaves a commit undetected with no sign; ref updates also arrive as bursts of lock-file renames the filter and debounce must absorb.

The extension reads the API of the built-in Git extension (`vscode.extensions.getExtension('vscode.git')`, `exports.getAPI(1)`, typed by a copied `git.d.ts`, with no `extensionDependencies` entry), picks the repository whose `rootUri` is the project root (waiting on `onDidOpenRepository` when it opens later), and on `repository.state.onDidChange` compares `state.HEAD`'s commit and name with the last seen, handing a full re-read to the existing debounce only when either moved. When the API is unavailable or never opens the repository, nothing is watched and Refresh stays the only way to pick up an outside change. Git's own parsing does the work: the Git extension already watches the git directory and handles worktrees, packed refs, and ref backends, and its `HEAD` commit lets the extension re-read exactly when the commit moved rather than on every file event. Detection depends on another extension's state the user controls: with `git.enabled` off, the Git extension disabled or inactive (as in a workspace it does not run in), or the repository not opened by its auto-detection, the change goes unnoticed silently; the API's typings are not in `@types/vscode` and must be copied and kept in step, `state.onDidChange` fires on every working-tree change, and the page tests need a stand-in for the API.

The built-in Git extension's API, as in the option above, is the primary signal, re-reading on a moved `HEAD` commit or name; when the extension is absent, disabled, or has not opened the project's repository, the extension instead creates the git-directory watcher over `HEAD`, `refs/heads/**`, and `packed-refs` described in the first option, and switches back to the API once the repository opens there. Both paths hand a full re-read to the existing debounce. It detects outside changes in every setup either mechanism covers alone: the precise, layout-proof API signal where the Git extension is running, and a working watcher where it is not. It carries both mechanisms and their failure modes, plus the switching logic between them, so the code and its tests roughly double for the case of a disabled Git extension, and the fallback path still inherits the git-layout blind spots of the first option.

The extension watches no git file and reads no other extension: while the session's live read stands, it runs `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git symbolic-ref -q HEAD` from the project root on a fixed interval of a few seconds and when the window regains focus (`vscode.window.onDidChangeWindowState`), and hands a full re-read to the existing debounce only when either print differs from the last one. It asks git itself, through the same `execFile` call shape the extension already uses for `git log`, so it is right under every git layout, worktree, and ref backend and needs no other extension, with one comparison of two strings to test. It spawns a git process every few seconds for as long as the session lasts, even while nothing changes, and a commit is picked up only at the next tick, so the page lags by up to the interval; a longer interval trades that lag up against the idle cost.
